title: NATO Submarine Rescue System - Master Version
description:
The NATO Submarine Rescue System (NSRS) is a cooperative project between three NATO countries: France, Norway and the United Kingdom. It is designed to rescue personnel from submarines in distress and can dive to depths of up to 600 metres. It consists of three main parts: an intervention system, a rescue vehicle and a transfer under pressure system. It is the largest fly-away submarine rescue system and can dive up to six hours, four times a day. On each dive, it can rescue approximately 12 submariners, who will receive medical treatment in its facilities, if needed.
The NATO Submarine Rescue System is available to anyone on request and can be deployed almost anywhere in the world within 72 hours.
Footage includes: interview with Commander Ian Duncan, NATO Submarine Rescue System Programme Manager, images from Exercise Dynamic Monarch 2017 and underwater filming of the exercise.
Teaser:Building on technology that rescued seven Russian submariners in 2005, three NATO Allies developed a cutting-edge underwater rescue system.

transcript.text: - Submarine rescue is a difficult business.
There are many unknowns and variables.
Each submarine accident is different.
^(solemn piano music)
The NATO submarine rescue system is unique,
it's the world's largest
flyaway transfer under pressure system.
Consists of three different parts.
^Firstly we have the intervention system which is a
remotely operated vehicle.
The next piece of equipment we have is a rescue vehicle,
which is a submarine that goes underneath the sea
to rescue the people,
and also a transfer under pressure system.
(solemn music)
We go down to the submarine.
We then mate with the submarine, we drain the water down
to make sure it has the hydrostatic pressure to hold
the submarine on top of the disabled submarine.
Once the hatch is opened, we can go inside the submarine.
We can lift casualties out of the submarine
and bring them into the rescue vehicle,
unload the personnel into the transfer under pressure
system where they can receive medical treatment.
(inaudible audio)
The NATO submarine rescue system has not been used
for real yet, thankfully.
However, the intervention system was used back in 2005
with the Russian submarine, the Pritz and we went down
and was able to cut the cables that were holding
the submarine on the sea bed and we saved the lives
of seven Russian submariners.
(piano music)
